concept.name: Stagflation
concept.definition: The simultaneous occurrence of high or rising inflation with stagnant output and elevated unemployment — a combination that contradicts the simple Phillips-curve trade-off. The term is identified with the 1970s U.S. experience, when inflation and unemployment rose together after the oil shocks.
concept.intuition: Stagflation is the worst of both worlds: the economy stops growing and jobs disappear while prices keep climbing, leaving policymakers with no painless option.
concept.mechanics: It typically arises when adverse supply shocks (e.g., the 1973 and 1979 oil crises) raise costs and prices while reducing output, and monetary accommodation of those shocks entrenches inflation expectations. Fighting unemployment with stimulus worsens inflation; fighting inflation with tightening worsens unemployment — the 1970s dilemma that ended only with the Volcker tightening of 1979-82.
concept.failure_modes: The label is often misapplied to any period of above-target inflation with mediocre growth; true stagflation requires sustained inflation together with economic stagnation, and the 1970s lesson (unstable Phillips trade-off) may not generalize to anchored-expectation regimes.
concept.misconceptions: Stagflation is not simply 'high inflation' or 'a recession'; its defining feature is the coexistence of both, which standard demand-management policy cannot fix from one side.
concept.example: By summer 1980, U.S. inflation was near 14.5% while unemployment exceeded 7.5% — the textbook stagflation that followed a decade of oil shocks and accommodative policy.

citations.source: Federal Reserve History — The Great Inflation
